---
title: "Presidency"
subtitle: "Building a democratic South Africa"
---

## Release and Negotiation

On 11 February 1990, Mandela walked free after 27 years in prison, greeted
by jubilant crowds and global media attention. President F. W. de Klerk had
lifted the ban on the ANC and other liberation movements shortly before,
opening the door to negotiations. Mandela became president of the ANC in
1991 and, alongside de Klerk, led years of difficult multi-party talks aimed
at ending apartheid and drafting a new, democratic constitution — negotiations
repeatedly threatened by political violence and mistrust on all sides.

In 1993, Mandela and de Klerk were jointly awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize**
"for their work for the peaceful termination of the apartheid regime, and
for laying the foundations for a new democratic South Africa."

## The 1994 Election

On 27 April 1994, South Africa held its first fully democratic election, in
which citizens of all races could vote. The ANC won a decisive majority, and
on 10 May 1994, Nelson Mandela was inaugurated as **South Africa's first
Black president**, with de Klerk serving as one of his deputy presidents in
a government of national unity.

::: {.quote-block}
"Never, never, and never again shall it be that this beautiful land will
again experience the oppression of one by another."
:::

## Reconciliation Over Retribution

Rather than pursue retribution against the architects and beneficiaries of
apartheid, Mandela championed a policy of national reconciliation. His
government established the **Truth and Reconciliation Commission**, chaired
by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, to investigate human rights abuses committed
during apartheid and offer conditional amnesty in exchange for full
disclosure — an approach aimed at healing rather than punishing a divided
nation.

Mandela also used symbolic gestures to unify the country, most famously
embracing the previously white-dominated Springbok rugby team during South
Africa's hosting and winning of the 1995 Rugby World Cup, an episode that
became emblematic of his approach to nation-building.

## Governance and Policy

As president, Mandela's government worked to redress the material
inequalities left by apartheid through programs such as the Reconstruction
and Development Programme, expanding access to housing, electricity, water,
and healthcare for Black South Africans. He also oversaw the adoption of a
new, progressive constitution in 1996, one of the first in the world to
explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

True to earlier promises, Mandela chose not to seek a second term, stepping
down in 1999 and handing power to his deputy, Thabo Mbeki — a peaceful
transition that reinforced South Africa's young democratic institutions.
